1. Executive summary and scorecard

PulsePantry is a mobile app concept that scans grocery receipts, logs each item with an estimated expiry date, warns users before food goes off, suggests recipes that use what is about to expire, and rewards people for wasting less.

This is the fourth revision. Since the last review the home screen gained a custom-made food-waste infographic, the dark theme now covers almost every screen (recipes, grocery list, rewards, profile and reviews are re-themed), the receipts screen shows a due date, a warning icon and a text label on every row, and a Figma kit with light and dark style frames, an icon set and reusable components has been added.

What still needs fixing is small but visible: the splash screen reads 'PantryPulse' while every other screen says 'PulsePantry'; no value is visible in the Rewards points box in either theme; Recipe 3 (light) still shows stray 'Prepa / No Use' text; the dark Scanner 'Details' cards are still white; and, by my calculation from the sampled colours, the gold logo text and icons on the dark-mode sage header sit at roughly 1.4 to 1.7:1 contrast, which fails WCAG.

1.1 What has improved

  • Home dashboard: a stock photo and quote were replaced by an original infographic (15 billion, 14 million, 1,071 and 357 days) in deep teal and green. It is on-brand and tells the story in one glance. It now needs an on-screen source and a text alternative.

  • Dark mode: from a light app with a dark shell to a nearly complete theme. Grocery list, recipes, rewards, profile and reviews now use dark surfaces with light text.

  • Receipts Info: every item row now shows the item, a due date, a warning icon and an add control in one repeated component, so expiry no longer depends on colour alone.

  • Scan History (Lidl, Tesco) is present in both themes and the source icons differ by capture method.

  • Design system: the Figma kit page now holds Light Mode and Dark Mode style frames, an icon frame and a component area (review card, settings list, authentication forms, warning cards). This is the strongest evidence of system thinking in the file.

3. Problem, solution and benefit

3.1 Problem

UK homes throw away about 4.4 million tonnes of edible food a year, creating around 16 million tonnes of greenhouse gases. WRAP puts the cost at about GBP 1,000 a year for an average household of four. (The original brief quotes GBP 700, a figure also used by Loughborough University in February 2026; use the current WRAP number and cite it.)

WRAP's 2026 survey found that 64% of people think some household food waste is inevitable, mainly because of spoilage and dates, unpredictable daily life, and difficulty with cooking and portions. People forget what they bought, do not notice items approaching expiry, and cannot turn leftovers into a meal.

3.2 Solution

PulsePantry turns a receipt into a live pantry. OCR reads the receipt, a food-category lookup estimates each item's expiry (receipts do not print expiry dates), and items are sorted into fridge, freezer and pantry. Users get a countdown and a push notification such as 'expiring in 2 days', then recipe suggestions built around those items. Marking an item 'used' or 'thrown away' closes the loop and feeds the waste metric and the rewards system.

3.3 Benefit

  • Saves money: fewer forgotten and expired items, and a grocery list built from low-stock items.

  • Saves time: one scan replaces manual stock-taking; recipes take under 30 minutes for busy parents.

  • Cuts waste and carbon, in line with the eco values of the target users.

  • Builds a habit through points, ranking and badges, which supports 30-day retention.

  • Inclusive by design: light and dark themes, text with icons, large targets, screen-reader labels.

6. User stories and acceptance criteria

ID

User story

Acceptance criteria (Given / When / Then)

US-01

As a user, I want to sign up, log in and reset a forgotten password so that my pantry is private and recoverable.

- Given I am new, when I enter name, age, email and a valid password, then my account is created and I am asked to set a 5-digit PIN.

- Given I forgot my password, when I request a reset and enter a new matching password, then I can log in with it.

- Given I enter a wrong PIN, when I try again, then I see a clear error and a way to get a new code.

US-02

As a shopper, I want to scan a receipt so that my items are logged without typing.

- Given camera access is allowed, when I capture a receipt, then items appear with estimated expiry within 5 seconds.

- Given camera access is denied, when I open the scanner, then I see a message and can upload a photo or import a PDF instead.

US-03

As a user, I want to correct a wrongly read item so that my inventory stays accurate.

- Given an item is flagged low-confidence, when I open it, then I can edit its name, category and expiry date.

- Given I save an edit, then the item updates and a confirmation is announced to screen readers.

US-04

As a user, I want an expiry alert so that I use food before it goes off.

- Given an item expires in 2 days, when the daily check runs, then I receive a notification naming the item.

- Given I open Receipts Info, then that item shows a warning icon, the text 'Expiring soon' and its due date.

US-05

As a cook, I want recipes that use expiring items so that I waste less.

- Given I have expiring items, when I open Recipes, then suggestions containing them are ranked first.

- Given I open a recipe, then ingredients and numbered steps are readable at 200% text size.

US-06

As a user, I want to mark items used or thrown away so that my waste is measured.

- Given an item, when I choose 'used' or 'thrown away', then it leaves the active list and is written to the waste log.

- Given I mark items used, then my points increase.

US-07

As a user, I want rewards so that I stay motivated to waste less.

- Given I reach a points threshold, then a badge is awarded and shown on Rewards.

- Given I open Rewards, then my points value and ranking are both visible.

US-08

As a user, I want day and night modes so that the app is comfortable to read in any light.

- Given I toggle the theme, then every screen changes together with no light cards left in dark mode.

- Given either theme, then all text meets 4.5:1 contrast.

US-09

As a user with access needs, I want scalable text, clear labels and large targets so that I can use the app independently.

- Given system text size is set to 200%, then no content is cut off.

- Given a screen reader is on, then each item is read as 'item name, expires date'.

- Given any button, then its target is at least 44 by 44 px.

US-10

As a shopper, I want a grocery list built from low-stock and out-of-stock items so that I buy only what I need.

- Given an item is low or out of stock, then it appears with status and 'Add to shopping list'.

- Given I search in the AI nutritionist box, then I get a text answer without leaving the list.

8. MVP requirements

The MVP tests one hypothesis: people who see expiry dates and get a recipe prompt will throw away less food. Everything that does not test this is deferred.

In scope for the MVP

  • Account creation, login and PIN

  • Receipt photo upload with OCR and manual correction

  • Category-based expiry estimates and inventory (fridge, freezer, pantry)

  • Expiry countdown and local push notification

  • Recipe suggestions from a curated set of about 30 recipes, ranked by expiring items

  • Used / thrown-away log

  • Light and dark mode

  • Accessibility baseline (scalable text, labels, contrast, targets)

Deliberately out of scope

  • Ranking and leaderboard

  • AI nutritionist assistant

  • Barcode scan and PDF import

  • Review system

  • Shared households

MVP success criteria

  • At least 20 pilot users log 3 or more shops in the first month

  • Median OCR correction rate under 15%

  • Thrown-away share falls by 20% or more between weeks 1 and 6

  • No critical WCAG AA failures

11. Technical documentation

11.1 Architecture and recommended stack

A mobile client calls a REST API. Receipt photos go to an OCR service; a parser turns raw text into lines and matches each to a FoodCategory whose default shelf life gives the expiry date. A scheduled job checks expiry daily and sends push notifications. The recipe engine matches recipe ingredients to the user's expiring categories. Original receipt images are deleted after parsing.

Layer

Choice

Why

Client

React Native (or Flutter)

One codebase for iOS and Android; fits existing React skills.

API

FastAPI (Python)

Fast to build, typed, and matches existing Python skills.

Database

PostgreSQL

Relational model in the ER diagram; date queries for expiry.

OCR

Managed OCR API, or Tesseract with pre-processing

Start managed for accuracy; measure correction rate before optimising.

Notifications

Firebase Cloud Messaging and APNs

Standard push delivery.

Scheduler

Daily job (cron or Celery beat)

Expiry checks and notification triggers.

Auth

JWT sessions, hashed PIN, optional biometrics

Meets WCAG 3.3.8 when an alternative to memorising a PIN exists.

CI/CD

GitHub Actions

Automated tests and builds.



11.2 Class diagram

Classes model the receipt-to-waste-log pipeline. FoodCategory holds the default shelf life used to estimate expiry, and InventoryItem owns the outcome that feeds the KPIs.

Figure 4: class diagram.

11.3 Entity relationship (ER) diagram

The ER diagram is the database design. INVENTORY_ITEM links to RECEIPT_LINE (nullable, for manual adds) and has at most one WASTE_LOG row, which is the source of the waste-reduction KPI.

Figure 5: entity relationship diagram.

11.4 Software development life cycle (SDLC) recommendation

Recommended model: Agile, using two-week Scrum-style sprints with prototype-first, MVP-first delivery (Kanban board for a solo developer).

Why this model fits

  • Key unknowns (OCR accuracy, shelf-life data quality, notification tolerance) can only be answered by real use, so short feedback loops beat a fixed up-front plan.

  • Requirements will change once real receipts arrive; Agile expects change.

  • The KPIs (correction rate, cook-through, retention) support a build-measure-learn cycle.

  • A solo or small team needs small, shippable increments and a visible backlog.

  • The Figma prototype already de-risks the UI, so sprints can go straight to the riskiest technical slice: receipt to expiry.

Phases and activities

Phase

Activities and outputs

Plan (sprint 0)

Backlog from user stories, MoSCoW priorities, definition of done including accessibility checks.

Design

Figma tokens and components; accessibility annotations; usability test of the prototype.

Build

Sprint 1: auth and inventory. Sprint 2: OCR and correction. Sprint 3: expiry and notifications. Sprint 4: recipes and waste log.

Test

Unit tests for the parser and expiry logic; device tests; screen-reader and contrast tests every sprint.

Release

TestFlight and Play internal track to about 20 pilot users.

Review and improve

Read KPIs; hold a retrospective; reprioritise. Add rewards and barcode only if the core loop works.



Models considered and rejected

Model

Verdict

Waterfall

Rejected. Fixed requirements up front do not suit an uncertain OCR problem and would delay user feedback.

V-model

Rejected. Its heavy verification suits safety-critical systems (see the DSO project), not a consumer app.

Spiral

Rejected. Formal risk cycles add overhead for a small MVP.




12. Design system

12.1 Colour theory

PulsePantry uses an analogous-warm palette anchored by cool greens. Forest green (#1D4823) and sage (#73A86C) carry freshness and sustainability; terracotta (#C9864B) and gold (#F1C84C) carry warmth and appetite; a warm cream (#FEFCE5) reduces glare and feels like paper.

The deep teal (#003948) used in the infographic sits almost opposite terracotta and gold on the colour wheel, so it acts as a complementary contrast that makes the statistics pop without adding a new hue family.

The 60-30-10 rule holds: about 60% neutral (cream in light mode, near-black green in dark mode), 30% greens and teal for structure, and 10% gold and terracotta for actions and highlights.

Dark mode is not an inversion. It keeps the same hue family on dark green surfaces (#14211A background, #1F2E24 cards) and keeps gold for actions, so the brand reads the same in both themes. The one exception is the header, which currently switches to a light sage that clashes with gold text (see 12.3).

12.4 Typography

The app uses a single humanist sans-serif (it looks like Noto Sans or Open Sans). One family keeps the interface calm and consistent. The kit already names styles for title, body, button and caption; the table below sets a scale for them (rename 'buttom' to 'button').

Style

Specification

Use

Title (bold)

24 px, bold (700), line height 32

Page titles such as SCAN RECEIPTS and REWARDS.

Title 2

20 px, semibold (600), line height 28

Section headings such as Details, Scan History.

Body

16 px regular, line height 24 (never below 14)

Recipe text, list content, descriptions.

Body bold

16 px semibold

Item names, values.

Button

14 to 16 px semibold

All calls to action; dark text on gold.

Caption

12 px regular, minimum

Timestamps, helper text. Avoid the smaller caption sizes seen in the recipe and table screens.



12.5 Styling strategies

  • Design tokens: colours and text styles stored as Figma variables so light and dark themes switch together.

  • 8-point spacing grid and consistent 12 to 16 px corner radius for cards, inputs and buttons.

  • Component library on the kit page: authentication forms, warning cards, review card, settings list, icon set.

  • Redundant status cues: every expiry state pairs icon, text and colour.

  • Progressive disclosure: the header menu and expandable fridge and drawer rows hide detail until needed.

  • Gamified visual language: badges and points use the same gold and terracotta accents as actions so rewards feel part of the brand.

  • State design: permission, logout and error dialogs designed in both themes.

12.6 Design structure and layout

  • Three-tab bottom navigation (Main, Scanner, Profile) within thumb reach, plus a header menu for secondary destinations.

  • Consistent page skeleton: header bar, back arrow and page title, primary content, action buttons.

  • Card-based layout for lists and recipes; tables reserved for the grocery list where comparison matters.

  • Content hierarchy follows the loop: scan, see items, act on expiring items, learn from results.

12.7 Components, iconography and imagery

  • Icons: one gold line-icon family plus a set of badge illustrations, kept in the kit's icon frame.

  • Imagery: original infographic and illustrations; recipe photography should be licensed or original, with alt text.

  • Buttons: gold fill with dark text; secondary actions as outlined or terracotta.

  • Dialogs: centred card with two clear actions (No / Yes, Cancel / OK).


13. WCAG 2.2 accessibility audit

Short answer: the design cannot honestly be called fully WCAG-compliant yet, and no static design can be certified. Conformance is tested on the built product with assistive technology. What can be said is that PulsePantry is designed toward WCAG 2.2 AA, that several criteria are likely met, and that the specific failures below are known and fixable.

The three biggest blockers are the dark-mode header contrast (about 1.4 to 1.7:1), the gold warning icon on terracotta rows (about 1.9:1), and small text in recipes, tables and captions.

Target: WCAG 2.2 Level AA (the current W3C Recommendation since 5 October 2023). Statuses: Likely pass, Needs test, Likely fail (fix), Not verifiable in a static design.

Criterion

Level

Status

Evidence from the screens and what to do

1.1.1 Non-text content

A

Needs test

Infographic, badges, food photos and icons need text alternatives. Add alt text notes to the kit.

1.3.1 Info and relationships

A

Needs test

The grocery table needs real header cells in the build; headings need a defined order.

1.4.1 Use of colour

A

Likely pass

Receipts Info pairs a warning icon, text and due date. Keep the same component on every list.

1.4.3 Contrast (minimum)

AA

Likely fail (fix)

Dark header text, white on terracotta and grey captions fail or are borderline (see 12.3).

1.4.4 Resize text

AA

Needs test

Fixed-height cards and tables may clip at 200%. Test with large system text.

1.4.11 Non-text contrast

AA

Likely fail (fix)

Gold warning icon on terracotta; terracotta inputs on cream have no strong border.

2.4.7 Focus visible

AA

Not verifiable

Add focus states for keyboard and switch users to the component kit.

2.5.8 Target size (minimum)

AA

Needs test

Header icons and the Upload Photo / Import PDF buttons look small. Make them at least 24 px, aiming for 44 px.

3.3.2 Labels or instructions

A

Likely pass

Forms have labels. Replace generic 'Submit' with specific labels such as 'Create account'.

3.3.7 Redundant entry

A

Needs test

Do not ask for the same details twice between sign-up and PIN set-up.

3.3.8 Accessible authentication (minimum)

AA

Needs test

The 5-digit PIN and code entry must allow paste and password managers, or offer biometrics as an alternative to memorising.

4.1.2 Name, role, value

A

Not verifiable

Annotate each control with its accessible name, especially icon-only header buttons.



14. Visual appeal evaluation and fix list

Overall visual appeal: 7.5 out of 10

The design is welcoming and clearly feels like one product: warm cream, deep green and terracotta suit a food app, and the custom infographic gives the home screen a memorable moment that generic apps lack. The dark theme now looks deliberate on most screens.

It loses points for density (small recipe and table text), a few unfinished details, and the bright sage dark header that reduces legibility of the brand name itself.

What works

  • Distinct, food-appropriate palette with real light and dark tokens

  • Original infographic and badge artwork instead of stock imagery

  • Complete flows including permission and logout states

  • Kit page shows design-system thinking

Fix

P1

Change the splash screen from 'PantryPulse' to 'PulsePantry' and check every logo and label.

Brand inconsistency on the first screen looks careless.

P1

Use a dark forest header in dark mode (#1D4823 or #2C4A38) with gold text.

Fixes the largest contrast failure and restores the logo's legibility.

P1

The key reward number is missing.

P1

Convert the dark Scanner 'Details' cards to dark surfaces (#1F2E24) with light text.

Finishes the dark theme.

P2

15. Results, next steps and interview talking points

Overall result

  • A complete, documented mobile product concept with light and dark themes and a design-system kit.

  • A closed-loop core idea (scan, expiry, alert, recipe, log outcome) that differentiates it from simple trackers.

  • Evidence of iteration: three review passes with specific, fixable findings.

  • Technical documentation (requirements, class and ER diagrams, SDLC) that shows product-analyst thinking.

Next steps

  • Complete the P1 fixes, then re-run a contrast check.

  • Run 5 usability tests and add findings, quotes and the changes they caused.

  • Add empty states, the item edit screen and screen-reader annotations.

  • Optionally build the MVP (React Native and FastAPI) to show design and code together.

Interview talking points

  • 'I found my own accessibility failures with a contrast audit and fixed them in two passes.'

  • 'The closed loop from expiry alert to used or thrown away is what lets the app measure waste, not just track it.'

  • 'I chose Agile because OCR accuracy is the biggest unknown and only real receipts can answer it.'

  • 'Dark mode used tokens, so light and dark switch together.'
